points_json.example: A doctor who diagnoses every stomach ache as appendicitis because she just saw three appendicitis cases this week.
points_json.point: Heuristics are mental shortcuts that speed up thinking but can mislead us. The availability heuristic judges likelihood by how easily examples come to mind — dramatic events (plane crashes) feel common, while quiet killers (diabetes) feel rare.

points_json.example: A shopkeeper prices a shirt at 999 instead of 1000 because the first number seen pulls all later judgments toward it.
points_json.point: The anchoring effect: the first number or idea we meet becomes a reference point. The representativeness heuristic judges by similarity to a stereotype — assuming a quiet book-lover must be a librarian, not a salesperson.

points_json.example: An investor who refuses to sell a losing stock because 'I've already put so much money in.'
points_json.point: Common decision traps: confirmation bias (seeking only information that agrees with us), the sunk-cost fallacy (throwing good money after bad because of past investment), and overconfidence (believing our judgments are better than they are).

points_json.example: A student stuck on a math problem takes a walk — the answer pops up in the shower.
points_json.point: Problem solving has stages: preparation (understanding the problem), incubation (the unconscious works while you rest), illumination (the aha moment), and verification (checking the solution). Breaks genuinely help creativity.

points_json.example: Using a shoe as a hammer when no hammer is around — or failing to, because you only see the shoe as footwear.
points_json.point: Functional fixedness is seeing objects only in their usual role, which blocks creative solutions. Mental set is sticking to a familiar method even when a better one exists — like always using the long route because it worked once.

points_json.example: A manager who lists pros and cons of two job offers, weighs them, and picks the better one.
points_json.point: Algorithms are step-by-step rules that guarantee a solution (trying every key on a keyring) but are slow. Heuristics are fast but can fail. Means-ends analysis breaks a goal into smaller steps, working backward from the target.

points_json.example: Framing: '90% survival rate' sounds good, '10% death rate' sounds terrible — same surgery, different choice.
points_json.point: How a choice is framed changes the decision. People avoid risk with gains (take the sure $100 over a 50% chance of $250) but chase risk with losses (gamble to avoid a sure loss) — this is prospect theory (Kahneman and Tversky).

points_json.example: A chess master who instantly sees the right move that a beginner cannot find after 10 minutes.
points_json.point: Expertise changes thinking: experts see meaningful patterns, organize knowledge deeply, and solve problems forward from principles — while beginners work backward from the goal and get lost in details. This comes from about 10 years of deliberate practice.

summary: How the mind solves problems — and the shortcuts that trick it. Heuristics, biases, creativity blocks, and decision traps, all in simple words with examples.
title: Thinking, Problem Solving and Decision Making

points_json.example: A student who scores average on IQ tests but reads people's emotions brilliantly and leads every group project.
points_json.point: Intelligence is more than one test score. Spearman proposed a general intelligence factor (g) behind all mental tasks. Thurstone argued for 7 primary abilities like verbal, numerical, and spatial skill. Modern views accept both — a general ability plus specific talents.

points_json.example: A street-smart vendor who cannot read but calculates complex change instantly and negotiates brilliantly.
points_json.point: Sternberg's triarchic theory: analytical intelligence (book smarts, tests), creative intelligence (new ideas), and practical intelligence (street smarts, everyday problem-solving). Success needs all three, not just exam skills.

points_json.example: A musician, an athlete, a poet, and a mathematician — all intelligent in completely different ways.
points_json.point: Gardner's multiple intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, spatial, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalistic. Schools overvalue the first two and ignore the rest.

points_json.example: A manager who stays calm when a client shouts, understands the real complaint, and resolves it gracefully.
points_json.point: Emotional intelligence (Goleman): recognizing your own emotions, managing them, motivating yourself, reading others' emotions (empathy), and handling relationships. It predicts job success as strongly as IQ in many fields.

points_json.example: Two children with the same IQ score — one raised with books and conversation thrives, the other in neglect struggles.
points_json.point: Nature and nurture both matter: intelligence is about 50–80% heritable, but environment decides how genes express. Good nutrition, schooling, and stimulating homes raise scores; poverty and neglect lower them. The Flynn effect: average IQ rises about 3 points per decade worldwide.

points_json.example: A 10-year-old who solves problems like an average 13-year-old has a mental age of 13.
points_json.point: Binet created the first intelligence test to find children needing help. IQ was mental age divided by chronological age, times 100. Modern tests (WAIS, WISC) compare you to same-age peers — average is 100, and about 68% of people score between 85 and 115.

points_json.example: A test that asks only cricket questions would call a brilliant footballer unintelligent.
points_json.point: Good tests need reliability (same result each time) and validity (measuring what they claim). Intelligence tests are criticized for cultural bias — favoring the language and experiences of one group — and for narrowing human worth to one number.

points_json.example: A dyslexic student who fails written exams but builds working machines from scrap.
points_json.point: Learning disabilities (dyslexia, dyscalculia) are not low intelligence — the brain processes specific inputs differently. With the right support, these students often excel. Intelligence and school performance are not the same thing.

summary: What does it really mean to be smart? From IQ tests to emotional intelligence and multiple intelligences — the big theories explained simply.
title: Intelligence: Theories and Testing

points_json.example: In a lift, everyone faces the back wall — you turn around too, though the door is in front.
points_json.point: Conformity means changing behavior to match the group. Asch's line experiment showed 75% of people gave an obviously wrong answer at least once just because everyone else did. We conform to be liked (normative influence) and to be right (informational influence).

points_json.example: A nurse who knows the doctor's dose looks wrong but stays silent because the whole team agreed.
points_json.point: Conformity grows with unanimous groups, difficult tasks, and low self-confidence. One ally who disagrees cuts conformity sharply. Culture matters too — collectivist societies conform more than individualist ones.

points_json.example: Ordinary people delivered what they believed were dangerous electric shocks to a stranger, just because a man in a lab coat said 'please continue.'
points_json.point: Milgram's obedience study: 65% of participants obeyed orders to shock a learner to the maximum, showing ordinary people can do harm under authority. Distance from the victim and closeness of the authority figure increased obedience.

points_json.example: A soldier ordered to harm civilians faces the same conflict Milgram's participants felt — sweating, protesting, yet obeying.
points_json.point: Why we obey: we enter an 'agentic state' where we feel like the authority's instrument, not responsible. Gradual steps (foot-in-the-door) make the next order easier. The lesson: evil often comes from obedience, not monsters.

points_json.example: In 1971, students assigned as 'guards' became cruel within days in a fake prison basement.
points_json.point: Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment showed how fast social roles corrupt — guards turned abusive, prisoners broke down. It was stopped after 6 days. Critics note demand characteristics, but the power of situations remains the lesson.

points_json.example: A salesman who first asks you to sign a petition, then asks for a donation — and you agree.
points_json.point: Persuasion tricks: foot-in-the-door (small request first), door-in-the-face (huge request first, then a smaller one feels reasonable), lowball (agree, then the price rises), and reciprocity (free sample makes you feel you owe a purchase).

points_json.example: A charismatic leader wins votes with emotional stories; an expert wins with facts and data.
points_json.point: The elaboration likelihood model: the central route (logic, evidence) persuades when people think carefully and creates lasting change. The peripheral route (attractiveness, celebrity, slogans) works when people don't think deeply — and fades fast.

points_json.example: After a heated debate, both sides leave more extreme than they arrived.
points_json.point: Group polarization: discussion pushes groups toward extremes. Groupthink is worse — the desire for harmony kills dissent, causing disasters. The cure: a designated devil's advocate and leaders who speak last.

summary: Why good people follow the crowd — and how persuaders exploit it. Asch, Milgram, Zimbardo, and the science of influence in simple words.
title: Conformity, Obedience and Persuasion

points_json.example: A baby who cries when mother leaves the room, then smiles and reaches out when she returns.
points_json.point: Attachment is the deep emotional bond between infant and caregiver. Bowlby said it is a survival system — babies who stay close to caregivers survive. Harlow's monkey experiments proved contact comfort matters more than food: baby monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother over a wire feeding mother.

points_json.example: In the Strange Situation test, a securely attached toddler explores happily, is upset when mother leaves, and is comforted when she returns.
points_json.point: Ainsworth's Strange Situation revealed 3 main styles. Secure attachment (about 65%): the child uses the parent as a safe base. Avoidant: the child ignores the parent, hiding distress. Resistant/ambivalent: the child is clingy yet angry, hard to comfort.

points_json.example: A 30-year-old who trusts partners easily versus one who panics at any sign of distance.
points_json.point: Attachment styles persist: secure adults have healthy relationships; anxious adults fear abandonment and need constant reassurance; avoidant adults distrust closeness and value independence above intimacy. But styles can change with healing relationships.

points_json.example: A father who consistently feeds, soothes, and plays with his baby builds secure attachment day by day.
points_json.point: Sensitive, responsive caregiving builds secure attachment — noticing the baby's signals and responding warmly. It is not about perfection; even 30% attuned responses build security. Neglect or frightening parenting breeds insecure styles.

points_json.example: An orphanage baby who rocks alone for hours, flinching from human touch.
points_json.point: Without attachment, children suffer: Romanian orphanage studies showed severe neglect causes stunted growth, cognitive delays, and reactive attachment disorder. But early adoption can remarkably reverse much of the damage.

points_json.example: A teenager who argues with parents yet calls her mother first with good news.
points_json.point: Attachment in adolescence shifts toward peers and romance, but parents remain the safe base. Teens with secure attachment explore more, take healthier risks, and handle breakups better.

points_json.example: A new mother who feels irritated by her crying baby, then guilty about it.
points_json.point: Adult attachment shapes parenting: secure parents raise secure children, continuing the cycle. The good news — becoming aware of your own style is the first step to breaking an insecure cycle with your children.

summary: The bond that shapes every relationship you'll ever have. Bowlby, Ainsworth, attachment styles from crib to adult romance — in simple words.
title: Attachment Across the Lifespan

points_json.example: A student who catches every cold during exam season, though she was healthy all semester.
points_json.point: Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI) studies how the mind, brain, and immune system talk to each other. Chronic stress raises cortisol, which suppresses immune cells — stressed people catch more colds, heal wounds slower, and respond weaker to vaccines.

points_json.example: A caregiver looking after a spouse with Alzheimer's for years shows weaker immune responses and slower wound healing.
points_json.point: Landmark finding: long-term caregivers and lonely people have measurably weaker immunity. Loneliness is as damaging to health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day — social connection is literally medicine.

points_json.example: Two people face the same deadline — one sees a challenge and thrives, the other sees a threat and gets sick.
points_json.point: Lazarus's model: stress depends on appraisal. Primary appraisal asks 'is this a threat?' Secondary appraisal asks 'can I cope?' The same event stresses one person and excites another — mindset changes biology.

points_json.example: A manager with no control over impossible targets develops high blood pressure within a year.
points_json.point: What makes stress toxic: lack of control, unpredictability, and no social support. High-demand, low-control jobs produce the most heart disease. Burnout — exhaustion, cynicism, inefficiency — is now an official occupational phenomenon.

points_json.example: A heart patient who practices daily relaxation has fewer second heart attacks than one who doesn't.
points_json.point: Type A personality (hostile, time-urgent) raises heart disease risk — hostility is the toxic ingredient. Managing stress through exercise, relaxation, and social support genuinely protects the heart.

points_json.example: A cancer patient who joins a support group reports less pain and better mood than one who faces it alone.
points_json.point: Coping styles: problem-focused coping fixes the issue (planning, action); emotion-focused coping soothes feelings (venting, reframing). Both help at the right time — but denial and avoidance backfire long-term.

points_json.example: A woman who writes about her worries for 15 minutes daily visits the doctor half as often.
points_json.point: Proven stress fighters: regular exercise (as effective as medicine for mild depression), 7–9 hours of sleep, expressive writing, mindfulness meditation, and strong relationships. Small daily habits beat occasional heroic efforts.

points_json.example: Hospital patients with a view of trees recover faster and need less pain medicine than those facing brick walls.
points_json.point: Health psychology in action: hospital design, doctor-patient communication, and patient beliefs all change outcomes. The placebo effect proves expectation alone can trigger real healing chemistry.

summary: How stress gets under your skin — literally. The mind-immune connection, why loneliness harms health, and science-backed ways to stay well.
title: Stress, Immunity and Health

points_json.example: A patient who free-associates about a dream of missing a train, and realizes it connects to fear of failing her exams.
points_json.point: Psychoanalysis (Freud): problems come from unconscious conflicts, often rooted in childhood. Tools include free association, dream analysis, and exploring transference (feelings toward the therapist that mirror past relationships). It is long, deep, and expensive.

points_json.example: A depressed student learns to catch the thought 'I'm a failure' and replace it with 'I failed one test; I can prepare better.'
points_json.point: CBT (Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy) is the most researched therapy: it finds the link between thoughts, feelings, and actions, then changes distorted thoughts and unhelpful behaviors. Structured, short-term, and highly effective for anxiety and depression.

points_json.example: A therapist who listens warmly without judging, reflecting the client's feelings: 'It sounds like you felt invisible in that moment.'
points_json.point: Humanistic therapy (Rogers): the therapist offers unconditional positive regard, empathy, and genuineness. The belief: people naturally grow toward health if given a safe, accepting space. Client-centered and non-directive.

points_json.example: A couple who fights daily learns to schedule calm weekly talks and reward kind behavior.
points_json.point: Behavior therapy applies learning principles: systematic desensitization for phobias, exposure for OCD, reinforcement for desired behavior. No deep digging — just changing the behavior patterns that maintain problems.

points_json.example: A family where a teenager's rebellion is really the parents' marriage conflict in disguise.
points_json.point: Family and couples therapy treats the system, not just the person. Structural therapy rearranges family roles; emotionally focused therapy rebuilds attachment bonds between partners. The identified patient is often the family's symptom-bearer.

points_json.example: A group of socially anxious strangers who realize 'I'm not the only one' in their first session.
points_json.point: Group therapy: cheaper and powerful — members learn they are not alone, practice social skills live, and get feedback from peers. Especially effective for addiction, grief, and social anxiety.

points_json.example: A psychiatrist who prescribes an SSRI for depression while the psychologist provides CBT alongside.
points_json.point: Biomedical therapy uses medicines: antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, anti-anxiety drugs. Best combined with psychotherapy for moderate-to-severe disorders. ECT (brief controlled seizures under anesthesia) helps severe treatment-resistant depression.

points_json.example: A therapist who blends CBT thought records with mindfulness meditation and cultural values.
points_json.point: Modern trends: integrative therapy mixes approaches for each person, mindfulness-based therapies (MBCT, ACT) add acceptance to change, and teletherapy has made help accessible worldwide. The therapeutic alliance — trust in the therapist — predicts success more than any technique.

summary: From Freud's couch to modern CBT — how each major therapy works, what it treats best, and why the relationship matters most.
title: Schools of Psychotherapy

points_json.example: You don't notice your watch on your wrist until someone mentions it.
points_json.point: Sensation is the raw signal — eyes, ears, skin converting energy into neural impulses. Perception is the brain's interpretation of those signals. Sensory adaptation tunes out constant stimuli (your watch, background hum) so you notice change.

points_json.example: A whisper in a quiet library versus the same whisper at a loud wedding.
points_json.point: The absolute threshold is the faintest detectable signal. The difference threshold (just noticeable difference) follows Weber's law — it is proportional: you notice a 1 kg change in a 10 kg bag, but need 10 kg change in a 100 kg bag.

points_json.example: A radiologist who spots a tiny tumor others miss — and sometimes sees one that isn't there.
points_json.point: Signal detection theory: detecting signals depends on sensitivity plus decision bias. A cautious radiologist misses little but raises false alarms; a bold one misses more. Payoffs and expectations shift the threshold.

points_json.example: The same warm water feels hot after cold water, but cool after hot water.
points_json.point: Our senses measure change, not absolutes. Sensory adaptation, contrast effects, and afterimages (staring at a flag then seeing its ghost in opposite colors) all show perception is relative and constructed.

points_json.example: You hear your name across a noisy party you were ignoring.
points_json.point: Selective attention filters the flood — the cocktail party effect lets you track one conversation in noise. But inattentional blindness is startling: half of viewers miss a gorilla walking through a basketball game when counting passes.

points_json.example: A coin looks round even seen at an angle; a door looks rectangular even when half-open.
points_json.point: Perceptual constancies keep the world stable: shape, size, and color constancy let you recognize objects despite changing angles, distances, and lighting. Without them, every head turn would remake reality.

points_json.example: The Müller-Lyer illusion: two equal lines look different lengths because of arrow fins.
points_json.point: The Gestalt principles explain how we group sensations: proximity, similarity, continuity, closure (seeing a whole circle from broken arcs), and figure-ground (vase or faces?). The whole is different from the sum of its parts.

points_json.example: Sailors who expect to see a ship spot one in fog where others see nothing.
points_json.point: Perception is active construction: bottom-up processing builds from raw senses, top-down processing applies expectations and knowledge. Culture, emotion, and motivation all shape what we literally see.

summary: How your brain builds reality from raw signals. Thresholds, illusions, attention, and the Gestalt rules — the hidden machinery of seeing and hearing.
title: Sensation and Perception

points_json.example: A lottery winner who is thrilled for 3 months, then returns to her old happiness level.
points_json.point: The hedonic treadmill: we adapt to good and bad events and return to a happiness set point. Lottery winners and accident victims both drift back toward their baseline within a year — circumstances matter less than we think.

points_json.example: A volunteer who spends Saturdays teaching street children reports deeper joy than a bonus ever gave her.
points_json.point: Seligman's PERMA model of well-being: Positive emotions, Engagement (flow), Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment. Lasting happiness comes from engagement and meaning, not just pleasure — the pleasant life versus the meaningful life.

points_json.example: A surgeon who loses track of time during a complex operation — hungry, tired, but completely absorbed.
points_json.point: Flow (Csikszentmihalyi) is total absorption when challenge matches skill — time vanishes, self-consciousness drops. It is the most satisfying human experience, found in sports, art, work, and even studying when the level is right.

points_json.example: Two patients with the same diagnosis — the optimistic one follows treatment and recovers faster.
points_json.point: Learned optimism (Seligman): optimists explain bad events as temporary and specific ('this failed because I didn't prepare'), pessimists as permanent and personal ('I always fail'). Optimism can be trained and improves health.

points_json.example: A community that rebuilds stronger after a flood, with neighbors closer than before.
points_json.point: Resilience is bouncing back from adversity — built from supportive relationships, realistic optimism, problem-solving skills, and self-care. Post-traumatic growth: many survivors report deeper meaning and stronger bonds after hardship.

points_json.example: A student who writes down 3 good things each night feels measurably happier in 3 weeks.
points_json.point: Positive psychology interventions that work: gratitude journaling, savoring good moments, performing kind acts, using signature strengths in new ways, and mindfulness. Small, consistent practices beat grand resolutions.

points_json.example: A nurse who finds deep purpose in comforting patients, beyond any paycheck.
points_json.point: Meaning beats money: beyond basic needs, more income barely raises happiness. Strong relationships are the top predictor — the 80-year Harvard study found warm connections keep people happiest and healthiest.

points_json.example: A man who forgives his father's harshness and feels a weight lift after decades.
points_json.point: Forgiveness and compassion free the forgiver most — lowering stress, blood pressure, and depression. Self-compassion (treating yourself as you would a friend) beats harsh self-criticism for motivation and growth.

summary: The science of what makes life worth living. Happiness myths, flow, resilience, gratitude — evidence-based ways to build a good life.
title: Positive Psychology: Happiness and Resilience
